issues.legal_issue: A court considering an application for interim protection in an arbitration is not strictly bound by the procedural requirements for attachment before judgment and may secure a claim where the applicable interim-relief considerations are satisfied.
material_facts: The applicant sought interim orders securing claims for the return of refundable security deposits paid by a company that had entered insolvency proceedings.
The respondents resisted relief by relying on internal arrangements under which the deposits had allegedly been applied towards debts owed to third parties.
The High Court found a prima facie case and ordered the respondents to deposit the claimed amounts or furnish bank guarantees.
The respondents’ disclosures showed substantial indebtedness and, in one instance, only one disclosed asset, which was encumbered.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the interim security orders and dismissed the appeals, holding that the court’s power to grant interim protection is not defeated by strict application of the procedural requirements for attachment before judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 empowers a court to secure the amount in dispute and to grant other interim protection that is just and convenient. The court must have regard to the basic principles of procedural law, including the principles underlying Order 38 Rule 5 and Orders 39 Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but is not strictly bound by their procedural requirements. Relief should be assessed by considering whether the applicant has a good prima facie case, whether the balance of convenience favours relief, and whether the applicant acted with reasonable expedition. Actual attempts to dispose of assets to defeat an award are not imperative; a strong possibility of diminution of assets may suffice. The Court relied on Adhunik Steels Ltd. v. Orissa Manganese and Minerals (P) Ltd., Ajay Singh v. Kal Airways Private Limited, Jagdish Ahuja v. Cupino Limited, Nimbus Communications Limited v. Board of Control for Cricket in India, Valentine Maritime Ltd. v. Kreuz Subsea Pte. Ltd., Deccan Chronicle Holdings Limited v. L & T Finance Ltd., and Srei Infrastructure Finance Limited v. Ravi Udyog Pvt. Ltd. It distinguished Raman Tech. & Process Engg. Co. v. Solanki Traders, which concerned attachment before judgment in a suit.

rule.if: arbitration_interim_protection_application and strong_prima_facie_case and balance_favors_interim_protection and applicant_acted_with_reasonable_expedition and strong_possibility_of_asset_diminution

predicates.arbitration_interim_protection_applicati: A party applied for interim protection in connection with an arbitration.
predicates.strong_prima_facie_case: The applicant’s material showed a strong prima facie basis for its claim.
predicates.balance_favors_interim_protection: The consequences of refusing relief for the applicant outweighed the consequences of granting it for the opponent.
predicates.applicant_acted_with_reasonable_expediti: The applicant sought interim protection with reasonable promptness.
predicates.strong_possibility_of_asset_diminution: The circumstances showed a strong possibility that the assets available to meet a future award would diminish.

issues.definition: When a party seeking interim protection in an arbitration establishes a strong prima facie case, a favourable balance of consequences, reasonable promptness, and a strong possibility of asset diminution, the court may secure the claim without requiring strict compliance with procedural requirements for attachment before judgment.

issues.legal_issue: A respondent’s lack of unencumbered assets does not, by itself, prevent a court from ordering interim security for a prima facie claim in an arbitration.
material_facts: The respondents disclosed that they were heavily indebted and had no asset other than an asset that was fully encumbered.
The applicant had a prima facie case for recovery of the refundable security deposits and risked being unable to enjoy the benefit of an award if the claims were not secured.
The High Court ordered the respondents to deposit the claimed amounts or provide bank guarantees.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the disclosure of no assets, or only fully encumbered assets, did not preclude an order securing the applicant’s claim and upheld the deposit or bank-guarantee orders.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 gives the court power to secure a claim in arbitration through equitable interim protection. Where the applicant has prima facie good chances of succeeding and may otherwise be unable to enjoy the fruits of an award, the fact that the opponent has no assets or only fully encumbered assets does not require dismissal of the application. The Court relied on the principles governing the broad, judicious exercise of interim-protection powers under Section 9, including those discussed in Jagdish Ahuja v. Cupino Limited and the authorities cited in the judgment.

predicates.arbitration_interim_protection_applicati: A party applied for interim protection in connection with an arbitration.
predicates.strong_prima_facie_claim: The applicant showed a prima facie strong prospect of succeeding on its claim.
predicates.award_may_be_unenforceable_without_secur: Without security, the applicant may be unable to obtain the benefit of a future award.
predicates.respondent_has_no_unencumbered_assets: The respondent disclosed no assets, or only assets that were encumbered.

issues.definition: If an arbitration applicant has a prima facie strong claim that may be uncollectable without security, the court may order security even when the respondent has no unencumbered assets.
